subject: microbiology
title: Primary immunodeficiency and transplant rejection

steps.tx: Antibody deficiencies declare themselves after maternal IgG wanes around six months, when recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections begin. **X linked agammaglobulinaemia** reflects absent Brutons tyrosine kinase with no B cells and all isotypes low, so live vaccines are avoided and **lifelong IVIG** is given. **Common variable immunodeficiency** presents in adults with low IgG with low IgA or IgM, autoimmunity, granulomas and bronchiectasis. Selective IgA deficiency is the commonest and largely silent, but anti IgA antibodies trigger anaphylaxis on transfusion, while hyper IgM from CD40 ligand defects brings opportunists with neutropenia.
steps.say: Antibody defects show up after six months, when the maternal IgG received at birth has waned and the infant starts getting recurrent sinus and lung infections with bacteria. Brutons agammaglobulinaemia means the child has no B cells and very low levels of every antibody type, so live vaccines must be avoided and monthly IVIG continues for life. Common variable immunodeficiency appears later in adults, with low IgG and autoimmunity alongside granulomas and damaged dilated bronchi. Selective IgA deficiency is common and usually harmless, but these patients can develop severe allergy when transfused because they carry anti IgA antibodies.

steps.tx: Combined and cellular defects strike earlier. **SCID** brings low T cells from ADA or cytokine chain defects, and **TREC screening** of newborns permits BMT before a live vaccine kills. **DiGeorge syndrome** (22q11 deletion) combines thymic aplasia, hypocalcaemia, heart defects and irradiated blood only. Wiskott Aldrich links eczema with platelet thrombocytopenia of small platelets and infections, and Job syndrome pairs high IgE with retained teeth and cold abscesses. Phagocyte defects finish the set: oxidase failure causes granulomatous disease (DHR test, catalase positive Aspergillus and Staph), while CD18 failure delays cord separation.
steps.say: Cellular defects are more dangerous than pure antibody defects because T cells defend against viruses and live vaccines. SCID brings very low T cells in infancy, and newborn TREC screening allows transplant before a live vaccine turns fatal. DiGeorge syndrome follows 22q11 deletion with absent thymus, low calcium, heart defects and a need for irradiated blood only. Wiskott Aldrich syndrome links eczema with small platelet bleeding and infections, while Job syndrome pairs high IgE with retained teeth and cold abscesses. Defective phagocytes complete the set: oxidase failure causes granulomatous disease with Aspergillus and Staph, diagnosed by the DHR test, while CD18 failure delays cord separation.

steps.tx: **Absent thymic shadow** on an infant chest film is a classic clue to T cell deficiency. The main film shows a narrow superior mediastinum without the normal sail shaped thymus, while the inset reminds you what the healthy **thymic sail sign** looks like. Such a child with recurrent viral, fungal or opportunistic infections should make you suspect **SCID** or DiGeorge syndrome, confirm lymphocyte subsets and act fast, because live vaccines can kill and transplant cannot wait.
steps.say: Look at this chest film alongside the normal inset. The sick infant has a narrow upper mediastinum with no thymic shadow, while the healthy baby shows the broad sail shaped thymus fanning from the mediastinum. An absent thymus in a baby with repeated viral or fungal infections points toward severe T cell deficiency such as SCID or DiGeorge syndrome. Examiners love this sign because it is visible long before fancy blood reports arrive, and it demands urgent immunology referral with strict avoidance of live vaccines.

steps.tx: Rejection keeps its own clock. **Hyperacute rejection** strikes in minutes from preformed ABO or HLA antibodies, with fibrinoid necrosis and thrombosis, so the graft is removed. **Acute cellular rejection** arrives over weeks to months as T cells invade tubules, and it responds to steroids or ATG. Acute humoral rejection shows antibodies with C4d staining and needs plasmapheresis plus IVIG and rituximab, while chronic rejection brings vasculopathy and fibrosis needing retransplantation. Prevention needs ABO compatibility, **HLA matching** with DR first, crossmatch by complement and flow, and desensitisation to lower panel reactivity.
steps.say: Rejection announces itself by timing, and the diagram fixes each type to its clock. Hyperacute rejection hits within minutes because preformed antibodies were already waiting, so the mottled graft must come out at once. Acute cellular rejection builds over weeks as T cells invade the tubules, and it usually melts away with pulse steroids or ATG. Humoral rejection is flagged by donor antibodies and C4d on biopsy and needs plasma exchange with IVIG, while chronic rejection scars vessels over years until retransplantation is the only answer. Matching starts before surgery with ABO compatibility, HLA typing led by DR, crossmatch and desensitisation.

steps.tx: Disease can run in reverse when the graft attacks its host. **Acute graft versus host disease** erupts within 100 days of transplant with skin rash, gut diarrhoea and liver cholestasis, while chronic disease brings sicca dryness, scleroderma skin and bronchiolitis obliterans. Irradiated blood prevents transfusion associated disease in these hosts. Control rests on **calcineurin inhibitors** such as ciclosporin and tacrolimus, which injure kidneys and cause tremor with diabetes, plus mycophenolate or azathioprine, sirolimus, steroids and basiliximab induction. Levels need monitoring because oversuppression invites infection and EBV driven **PTLD**.
steps.say: Sometimes the transplant attacks the patient instead of the other way round. Acute graft versus host disease appears within one hundred days with a skin rash, watery diarrhoea and jaundice from liver injury, while chronic disease dries the eyes and mouth, hardens the skin and narrows the small airways. Irradiated blood products prevent the transfusion linked form in weak hosts. Long term control uses ciclosporin or tacrolimus, which can damage the kidney and cause tremor and diabetes, alongside mycophenolate, sirolimus, steroids and basiliximab induction. Levels need regular checks because excess suppression invites infections and EBV driven lymphoma.
